name: ChartQA
description: A large-scale benchmark for question answering about charts with visual and logical reasoning, covering 9,608 human-written questions and 23,111 questions generated from human-written chart summaries. The benchmark consists of 20,882 charts curated from four different online sources (Statista, Pew Research, Our World In Data, and OECD) to ensure variety in visual styles and topics. Questions focus on compositional and visual reasoning, including arithmetic and logical operations over chart data.
creator: Ahmed Masry, Do Xuan Long, Jia Qing Tan, Shafiq Joty, Enamul Hoque
citeAs: Masry, A., Long, D. X., Tan, J. Q., Joty, S., & Hoque, E. (2022). ChartQA: A Benchmark for Question Answering about Charts with Visual and Logical Reasoning. arXiv:2203.10244v1 [cs.CL].
rai:dataCollection: Charts were crawled from four different online sources: Statista (statista.com), Pew Research (pewresearch.org), Our World In Data or OWID (ourworldindata.org), and OECD (oecd.org). For the Pew dataset, only chart images were crawled since the underlying data tables are not available. For the other three sources, the underlying data tables, metadata (e.g., title, chart type), SVG files, and associated text descriptions were extracted. Bounding box information of different chart elements was extracted from SVG files to train data extraction models. Human-authored QA pairs were collected using Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT), and additional QA pairs were generated automatically from human-written Statista chart summaries using a fine-tuned T5 model.
rai:dataCollectionType: Web Scraping, Manual Human Curator, User-generated content data
rai:dataCollectionMissingData: For the Pew dataset, the underlying data tables are not available, so only chart images were crawled. Some machine-generated questions were found to be either incomplete or not answerable from the chart (e.g., questions requiring knowledge outside of the chart). A heuristic was applied to filter out such invalid questions by checking if the answer can be found in the chart data table.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Charts and associated data were collected from four online sources: Statista (economy, politics, industry topics), Pew Research (social and economic issues, demographic trends, public opinion), Our World In Data (global issues such as economy, finance, society), and OECD (reports and data analysis for policymaking). Human-written chart summaries from Statista were used to generate machine-based QA pairs.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: A T5 model was fine-tuned on the SQuAD QA dataset and applied to human-written chart summaries from Statista to automatically generate questions. The process involved two T5 models: one for answer extraction (trained on SQuAD passage-to-answer pairs) and one for answer-aware question generation (trained on SQuAD (passage, answer)-to-question pairs). A heuristic filter was applied to remove questions where the answer cannot be found in the chart data table. The test set of the machine-generated dataset was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For data extraction, the ChartOCR model was extended to output fully-structured data tables. The CRAFT model was used to recognize texts in chart elements. Data values were associated with text labels using positional and color information. For machine-generated questions, a heuristic filter removed questions where the answer could not be found in the chart data table. After filtering, 1,250 QA pairs were manually analyzed and 86.64% were found to be complete, answerable, and correct. The test set of machine-generated data was manually cleaned by removing invalid questions. Both human-written (ChartQA-H) and machine-generated (ChartQA-M) QA pairs were randomly split into train, validation, and test sets.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Human-authored QA pairs were collected via Amazon Mechanical Turk (AMT). In each HIT (Human Intelligent Task), workers verified two previously asked questions by other workers and provided two new QA pairs focusing on compositional questions (containing at least two mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes such as color, height, and length of graphical marks). For each chart, workers provided two questions with answers. The same questions were then answered by another annotator. If both workers' answers exactly matched, the answer was considered correct. Otherwise, answers were manually checked to select the final correct answer. Workers were required to have an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5,000 accomplished HITs, and were further filtered through a pre-test.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The agreement between crowd workers based on exact matches was 61.04%. However, exact match does not consider typos or lexical variations (e.g., '3$' vs '3 dollars', '86.33' vs '86.3'). A manual check of 500 random samples found the agreement to be 78.55% when considering typos and lexical variations. For machine-generated questions, 1,250 QA pairs were manually analyzed and 86.64% were found to be complete, answerable, and correct given the chart.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 2 questions per chart for human-authored QA pairs; each question answered by at least 2 annotators
rai:annotatorDemographics: Amazon Mechanical Turk workers with an acceptance rate of 95% and at least 5,000 accomplished HITs. Workers were compensated based on the minimum wage in the United States at the time ($7.25 USD per hour), receiving $0.60 USD per task (estimated 3-5 minutes per task). All annotations were anonymized to protect annotator privacy.
rai:machineAnnotationTools: T5 model fine-tuned on SQuAD for answer extraction and question generation; ChartOCR for automatic chart data extraction; CRAFT model for text recognition in chart elements; Mask R-CNN with Resnet-101 for visual feature extraction
rai:dataSocialImpact: The models can be abused to mislead the public about chart content and implications. The dataset covers topics including politics, economy, health, and society. The benchmark is intended to help users analyze data visualizations through natural language question answering.
rai:dataBiases: Politics is a common topic among all sources but particularly in the Pew dataset where nearly half of charts are about U.S. Politics & Policy (45.4%). Bar charts are the most common chart type (79.4% simple, 29.6% complex among bar charts). The dataset is constructed from four specific online sources which may not represent all possible chart styles and topics.
rai:dataLimitations: Current models cannot effectively handle nested arithmetic operations. Performance decreases when the gold data table is not provided, highlighting challenges in automatic data extraction from real-world charts with diverse styles. The evaluation metric for chart data extraction does not take extracted textual tokens into consideration, which are much more noisy in real-world figures. Models may generate incorrect outputs and correctness cannot be guaranteed. The dataset is limited to bar, line, and pie chart types.
rai:dataUseCases: Training, validation, and testing of Chart Question Answering (ChartQA) systems. The benchmark is intended to evaluate visual and logical reasoning over charts, including compositional questions (requiring mathematical/logical operations) and visual questions (referring to visual attributes of chart elements). The dataset can serve as a benchmark for evaluating transformer-based QA models that combine visual features and data tables.
